html:
Theta-gamma during active behavior and REM

During movement, attentive exploration, and REM sleep, the hippocampus enters an "online" regime dominated by 6-10 Hz theta whose cycles organize local spiking and the nesting of faster (30-150 Hz) gamma bursts. Medial septal GABAergic pacemaker cells entrain hippocampal interneurons and pyramidal cells at theta, while hypothalamic inputs (notably the supramammillary nucleus) modulate theta frequency and gain-together setting the temporal backbone for hippocampal computation 1, 2, 3. Causally, suppressing septal GABAergic drive selectively during REM reduces hippocampal theta and impairs consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memories, establishing the behavioral importance of this state 4. A 2025 rat study records place cells during exploration (Figure) 133.

A hallmark of this regime is phase precession: as an animal traverses a place field, a place cell fires at progressively earlier phases of the ongoing theta cycle. Population-wise, this compresses a seconds-long trajectory into a  100-150 ms theta window, effectively time-ordering the recent past and near future within each cycle 5, 6, 7. Phase precession, first reported in rodent CA1 and then generalized across hippocampal-entorhinal circuits, has now been demonstrated in humans (including for non-spatial, goal-related representations), supporting a domain-general role in sequencing 7. The study examines place-cell phase precession (Figure).

These within-cycle orderings manifest as theta sequences-rapid sweeps of place-cell activity that span positions just behind and ahead of the animal. At decision points, CA3 and CA1 ensembles transiently represent alternative future paths, and theta sequences bias toward current goals when choices must be made 8, 9. Coordinated hippocampal and prefrontal sequences at multiple timescales link these within-theta "micro-simulations" to behavioral planning 10. As tasks become stereotyped, theta sequences become less exploratory, consistent with a transition from deliberation to habit 9, 11. A 2025 study examines theta sequences after a detour (Figure) 134. The gamma study analyzes theta sequences in rat CA1 (Figure).

Theta provides a phase-structured clock that both aligns spikes for Hebbian updates and sets the sign of those updates. Because theta sequences and theta-gamma nesting compress seconds of behavior into  100-150 ms cycles, presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes repeatedly fall within the  10-50 ms windows required for STDP. Moreover, the phase of theta gates plasticity: brief bursts at one CA1 theta phase drive LTP, whereas the opposite phase favors LTD, yielding alternating epochs of encoding vs. weakening within each cycle 12, 13. In models constrained by hippocampal physiology, STDP operating on phase-precessing inputs forms directed chains-and even successor-like predictive maps-within a handful of traversals 14.

Within each theta cycle, gamma-nested "item packets" segment assemblies into discrete subevents. Critically, CA1 couples to different afferents at different gamma sub-bands and theta phases: "slow" ( 30-50 Hz) gamma synchronizes CA3->CA1 interactions associated with retrieval of stored associations, whereas "fast" ( 60-100 Hz) gamma aligns entorhinal cortex->CA1 drive associated with current sensory input 15, 16, 17. Human and animal work shows that assigning different items or positions to distinct theta phases (via theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling) supports sequence encoding and order memory 18. The rat study examines slow-gamma phase precession (Figure).

Theta also synchronizes hippocampus with neocortical partners to broadcast and read out these sequences. Hippocampal-mPFC theta coherence increases at choice points and during rule acquisition; prefrontal units can show theta phase relationships and even phase precession tied to spatial variables. Across trials, coherent theta supports a shared positional code between CA1 and mPFC, linking hippocampal simulation to executive selection 19, 20, 21.

A key subcortical coordinator is thalamic nucleus reuniens, which reciprocally connects mPFC and hippocampus. Reuniens manipulations modulate mPFC-hippocampus theta coherence and extinction retrieval 22, and can transiently impose synchronized beta bursts for memory-guided decisions-evidence that thalamus flexibly switches interareal channels on top of the theta scaffold 23. Broader midline thalamic circuits help align the timing of hippocampo-prefrontal interactions during working memory and spatial tasks 24, 25.

Finally, theta in REM appears to re-use the same temporal code under different neuromodulatory conditions. Selective disruption of REM theta impairs contextual memory consolidation without abolishing REM per se 4, and convergent reviews argue that NREM ripples and REM theta play complementary roles-ripples for sharp, compressed reactivation; REM theta for integrative, schema-updating plasticity under high acetylcholine. Reports of theta-sequence-like organization during REM suggest that online sequence machinery is redeployed offline, albeit with different coupling to cortex than during wake 26.

In summary, theta provides the millisecond-precision temporal scaffold that turns distributed hippocampal activity into ordered sequences, gates plasticity through phase-specific STDP, and multiplexes input-output streams via gamma nesting. By synchronizing with prefrontal, entorhinal, and thalamic partners, the theta-gamma code binds items into episodes during exploration and reprocesses them during REM. Recent human MEG evidence links hippocampal theta power to goal distance during planning (Figure) 132. Theta–gamma coupling also increases as people approach a goal, with fast and slow gamma linked to novel and familiar paths (Figure).

Sharp-wave ripples during pauses, quiet wakefulness, and NREM sleep

Sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) are brief, highly synchronous population events generated when a CA3 population burst produces a large "sharp wave" in CA1 dendrites while fast ( 140-200 Hz in rodents;  80-120 Hz in humans) ripple oscillations ride in the CA1 pyramidal layer for  30-120 ms. Mechanistically, SWRs start as a build-up in the recurrent CA3 network; the CA3 surge drives CA1, where perisomatic PV-basket-cell-mediated inhibition phase-locks sparse pyramidal spiking at ripple frequency 27, 28, 29. This interneuron-pyramidal loop accounts for the striking temporal precision and for the fact that only a small subset of CA1 pyramids fire on any given cycle. SWRs occur most frequently in NREM sleep, less during quiet wake/immobility, and least during brief pauses in locomotion-precisely the "offline" windows that isolate plasticity from ongoing sensorimotor drive 30. The detour study examines offline replay (Figure).

Content-wise, SWRs compress recent or predictive experience into time-ordered "replay" sequences. In awake immobility, replay runs in reverse after rewards (assigning credit to the just-traveled path) and forward before movement (prospective planning), often depicting routes from the current position to a known goal 31, 32. Across tasks, awake hippocampal-prefrontal replay during SWRs distinguishes correct from incorrect choices, and its prevalence shifts from reverse->forward with learning, linking replay to evaluation and planning rather than mere recapitulation 33. Notably, some datasets emphasize that replay can reflect previously important but currently unattended paths, underscoring that replay content is not a simple mirror of the next action 34.

Several lines of causal evidence put SWRs on the critical path for memory. Disrupting ripple-locked spiking during post-learning rest or sleep impairs spatial learning 35, whereas prolonging naturally occurring long-duration ripples enhances memory 36. At the synaptic level, place-cell reactivation during ripples drives potentiation in downstream CA1, providing a mechanism for "stamping in" recent experience 37. Together, these results argue that SWRs are not epiphenomenal but instructive for consolidation and decision support.

SO-spindle-ripple cascades during NREM sleep

During NREM, sharp-wave ripples are embedded in a slow-oscillation->spindle->ripple hierarchy with clearly defined generators and timing. Slow oscillations (SOs) are <1 Hz alternations between cortical down-states (neuronal quiescence/hyperpolarization) and up-states (widespread depolarization), originating largely in neocortex and often propagating as traveling waves; the SO up-state increases cortical excitability and provides the coarse timing frame for memory transfer 38, 39, 40. Sleep spindles are brief waxing-waning sigma bursts ( 11-16 Hz,  0.5-2 s) generated by reciprocal loops between thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) interneurons and thalamocortical relay cells, with "slow" ( 9-12 Hz, frontal-dominant) and "fast" ( 12-15 Hz, centro-parietal) subtypes that occupy slightly different SO phases 41, 42, 43.

Human intracranial and scalp work shows the canonical nesting: SO up-states group spindles, and the troughs of those spindles, in turn, cluster hippocampal ripples ( 80-100 Hz in humans;  140-200 Hz in rodents), providing millisecond-precision "transfer slots" for compressed hippocampal content 44, 45. The directionality of this chain has been resolved at subcortical nodes: convergent cortical down-states lead thalamic down-states, which hyperpolarize thalamic cells and trigger spindles that are projected back to cortex on the down-to-up transition-exactly when ripples are most likely to be nested 46.

Causally, boosting the phase alignment within this triad improves memory: closed-loop auditory stimulation that delivers sounds in-phase with impending SO up-states amplifies SOs/spindles and enhances next-day recall, and optogenetically timing thalamic spindles in-phase with the SO up-state increases triple coupling and hippocampus-dependent memory; out-of-phase timing is ineffective or detrimental 47, 48, 49. Beyond mere coincidence, spindles appear to mediate hippocampal-neocortical communication most strongly during long-duration ripples and when prefrontal spindles are themselves locked to local SO up-states, linking the strength of nesting to the efficiency of systems consolidation 50. Quantitatively, human depth recordings demonstrate that ripple probability rises within the spindle window and that ripple power is phase-locked to spindle troughs while spindle power climbs toward the SO up-state, confirming a precise SO->spindle->ripple phase-amplitude cascade in hippocampus and cortex 45. Finally, prefrontal cortex is not a passive recipient: iEEG shows that prefrontal slow-waves and spindles can organize ripple-locked information transfer-consistent with a thalamo-cortical "gate" that schedules hippocampal broadcasts into cortico-cortical networks at the exact SO phase when plasticity and effective connectivity are maximal 51.

Together, these results elevate the SO-spindle-ripple triad from a correlational motif to a mechanistic clocked bus for systems consolidation: SOs set the frame, thalamic spindles carve high-gain channels, and ripples deliver compressed episodic content to targets poised for synaptic change 52.

In humans, ripples are not confined to hippocampus: brief  90 Hz cortical ripples appear across association cortex in sleep and quiet wake, often co-occurring with hippocampal ripples and increasing during successful recall. These widespread events frequently recruit default-mode-network hubs and track memory demands, suggesting that SWR-time broadcasting reaches cortex via both thalamocortical spindles and locally generated cortical ripples that bind distributed assemblies during reactivation 53, 54.

SWRs also interact with control systems. The thalamic nucleus reuniens, which links hippocampus and mPFC, modulates prefrontal-hippocampal coherence around offline states, positioning midline thalamus as a switchboard that helps route ripple-time content to executive networks 25, 55. Intriguingly, recent work in rodents shows brief prefrontal cortical ripples that can top-down suppress hippocampal reactivation-evidence that cortex is not a passive recipient but can gate or veto hippocampal outputs during offline computation 56.

A central organizing principle is prioritization. Replay frequency and direction are shaped by salience and learning stage-reverse replay scales with reward magnitude at the goal 57, while forward replay forecasts planned paths; normative models formalize this as prioritized memory access, where the utility of a replayed transition depends on predicted performance gain 58. New experiments show that awake SWRs preferentially sample informative fragments of experience, consistent with these theories 59.

Neuromodulators gate when the brain enters the SWR regime. Acetylcholine, high during online encoding, suppresses ripples; elevating septal cholinergic drive reduces SWR incidence and impairs working-memory performance, while ACh drops during ripple-rich offline periods. This state control helps segregate "write" and "replay" modes across the day-night cycle 60, 61.

Event Boundaries and Segmentation Dynamics

Continuous experience is parsed into events by detecting when the current situation model stops predicting incoming data and must be updated. In humans, these "event boundaries" elicit transient increases in hippocampal and default-mode network (DMN) activity during naturalistic viewing and listening, and boundary-evoked responses in posterior hippocampus predict later memory detail, especially in younger adults 62, 63, 64. Boundaries are not only detected when the sensory stream changes; similar boundary-like responses appear at internally generated context shifts during unguided recall, implying a common neural "context switch" signature for external and internal transitions 65, 66. Computationally, boundary probability correlates with Bayesian surprise derived from language-model predictions during narrated stories 67, supporting the idea that segmentation tracks model mismatch rather than low-level surprisal alone. Together, this work formalizes boundaries as update points in an online generative model, aligning perceptual segmentation with memory formation. The same study examines responses around event boundaries (Figure). The human study tracks activity before and after boundaries (Figure).

Hippocampal dynamics at boundaries are both selective and functional. fMRI and EEG show that boundaries trigger rapid reinstatement of the just-ended event, plausibly "packaging" it before a new model is initiated, and hippocampal offset responses scale with subsequent memory for the preceding episode 68, 69. In naturalistic studies, boundary strength modulates the magnitude of cortical pattern shifts and the hippocampal response 70; boundary-evoked hippocampal-PMN coupling at event offsets is especially predictive of durable memory for central narrative content 64. These observations converge on a boundary-centric consolidation step in which reinstatement and hippocampal-cortical interaction at the end of an event stabilize its representation. The study analyzes neural pattern changes (Figure). A rat experiment studies representations after a change in route (Figure).

Segmentation has structured consequences for how memories are organized. A consistent behavioral pattern is strengthened ordering and binding within events but impaired ordering across events; these cross-boundary costs are malleable and can reverse when retrieval cues reinstate the right context 71. The Event Horizon account and modern reviews integrate this by proposing that boundaries create separate situation models that facilitate access to cohesive "chunks," with context reinstatement determining whether items straddling a boundary integrate or dissociate 72. Recent work also indicates that goal shifts and task-set switches are sufficient to impose boundaries, emphasizing the agent- and goal-centric nature of event structure 73, 74. The analysis follows pattern changes through a boundary (Figure).

Importantly, boundaries are not only "cuts" but also integration points. During ongoing narratives, the brain selectively reactivates context-specific past information at event boundaries, retrieving only the prior episodes needed to interpret the present 66. Hippocampal mechanisms that support this "event conjunction" likely leverage theta-gamma organization to reconstruct a high-level model from the just-ended event and append new details as a related event begins 75. In line with this, the hippocampus contributes to constructing cross-event narratives, with posterior medial network partners supplying schematic structure 76.

Event structure also has a graph-theoretic footprint. When movies are converted into event networks, nodes with higher centrality-defined by denser semantic and causal linkages-are better remembered, elicit larger hippocampal boundary responses at encoding, and drive stronger DMN recruitment at recall 77. These central nodes function as hubs that knit local event segments into a global memory graph. Complementing this, behavioral modeling demonstrates that people search memories by "skipping" from boundary to boundary, using these hubs as access points, which explains efficient retrieval of long naturalistic episodes 78, 77.

What prompts boundaries? Beyond prediction error in perception and language, salient reward prediction errors create mnemonic boundaries that disrupt temporal integration across them 79; arousal-linked boundary effects track pupil-indexed locus coeruleus engagement at environmental changes 80. Boundaries also arise at subtask switches 73, environmental/scene changes 81, 74, and goal shifts, underscoring that segmentation is causation- and control-centric rather than purely sensory 82. Theoretical and empirical updates nuance classic prediction-error accounts by showing that contextual stability (and prospective knowledge about imminent changes) can also generate boundary-like segmentation even without surprise. A 2026 study compares human and model-derived event boundaries (Figure) 135. The 2026 study separates candidate boundary mechanisms (Figure).

At the mesoscale, segmentation dovetails with systems-level coordination and replay. During naturalistic movie watching with intracranial recordings, human hippocampal ripples concentrate at event boundaries while cortical ripples occur preferentially within events, suggesting a division of labor in which hippocampus tags segment ends and cortex processes intra-event content 83; coordinated ripple timing across temporal-hippocampal-frontal sites supports encoding 84. More broadly, replay-triggered activations seen at rest highlight that the same circuits enlisted at boundaries for online model-updating are reused offline to refine the event graph. The detour study compares offline and later representations (Figure).

Finally, the "engram" perspective reframes boundaries as times when membership in cell assemblies can be retuned. Across DG, CA3, CA1, mPFC and sensory cortices, engram composition is dynamic across consolidation and retrieval, with inhibitory plasticity shaping which neurons remain in the trace. Models with coordinated hippocampal-thalamic-cortical timescales reproduce engram turnover and predict that coupled reactivations at boundaries accelerate systems consolidation-linking segmentation, reinstatement, and long-term remodeling of memory substrates 85, 86, 87.

In summary, boundaries are algorithmic "commit-and-integrate" points where the brain (i) detects a model change via Bayesian surprise or goal/context shifts; (ii) rapidly reinstates relevant recent episodes and schema fragments to integrate them with the just-arrived evidence into an updated situation model; (iii) gates hippocampal-cortical communication to bind this integrated content-selectively strengthening central nodes and writing new cross-event links (causal, semantic, and goal-related) into the event graph; and (iv) schedules ripple- and spindle-coordinated interactions that both package the completed segment and propagate the newly integrated inferences to long-term stores. Framed this way, boundaries do not merely segment experience-they are constructive junctions that stitch episodes into narratives, update schemas and policies, and allocate fresh indices/pointers so future retrieval can flexibly jump from boundary to boundary for goal-directed inference over a hierarchical, causal network of events.

History

Traditional views of episodic thought saw it purely in terms of iconic forms of representation 88, meaning it preserves the structure and relationships of its inputs when they are retrieved (e.g encoding egocentric maze traversal in episodic memory would not lead to new routes being simulated episodically)

Modern neuroscience has elaborated upon this perspective, showing that the episodic memory system serves as a unified substrate for reconstructing past episodes, imagining future episodes, and simulating counterfactual episodes []; i.e, that the episodic memory system is actually a flexible event simulation system that has its generation process conditioned by task representations []

Episodic thought likely fits well into the Language of Thought (LoT) framework, which argues that mental representations have fundamental characteristics resembling linguistic structure, such as discrete components, predicate-argument structure, role-filler structure, and abstract content 89, 90. This point of view further speaks to the versatility of the episodic memory system and synthesizes the cognitive and psychological properties of episodic thought with findings in the neuroscience literature (e.g role-filler independence reflects two distinct "role" and "entity" streams of hippocampal inputs from the medial and lateral entorhinal cortex, respectively)

When the future utility of current stimuli is unknown, the safest bet is to over-encode rich episodes and decide later what to read out. Recent behavioral work shows that people preferentially rely on detailed episodic memories to guide choice precisely when future task demands are uncertain, consistent with the idea that EM stores high-fidelity event representations nonselectively so that any feature can be queried if it later proves relevant. Converging evidence indicates that environmental volatility/uncertainty shifts arbitration toward episodic retrieval over incremental (habit-like) learning, sharpening the decision benefit of those detailed traces 131, 125.
